# Methods

### Site description and experimental design

In 2015, a functional group removal experiment was established at twelve semi-natural grassland sites in Vestland county, Western Norway @fig-design. The sites were arranged in a climate grid spanning three temperature levels (6.5, 8.5, and 10.5 °C summer temperature) and four precipitation levels [700, 1500, 2100 and 2800 mm annual precipitation; based on gridded climate data by met.no; @vandvik2022role]. The target vegetation were south-facing, forb-rich semi-natural grasslands, where bedrock, slope, aspect, vegetation type, grazing regime and history were kept as similar as possible. [*add something on NiN types*]. All sites were moderately grazed before the experiment was established. To prevent grazing the experimental sites were fenced, and aboveground biomass was harvest inside the fence at the end of each growing season to prevent biomass accummulation inside the experimental site.

At each site, four experimental blocks with eight 25 x 25 cm plots were established (total n = 384 plots). The plots were permanantly marked with aluminium tubes in each corner for repeated observations and measurments. In a fully factorial removal experiment, the aboveground biomass of the three dominant plant functional groups was removed; forbs (including herbaceous forbs, pteridophytes, dwarf-shrubs, and small individuals of trees and shrubs), graminoids (grasses, sedges, and rushes) and bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, and hornworts). For eight years, the aboveground biomass was removed anually using sissors and tweezers removing the plants at ground level. In 2015 the biomass was removed once at peak growing season due to late snowmelt, while in 2016 and 2017 the biomass was removed twice (early and peak season) to prevent regrowth. For the remainder of the experiment, the biomass was only removed once at peak growing season. For more details see [@vandvik2022role].

![Study area, site selection, experimental design, and field sampling overview for the FunCaB plant functional group experiment. For detailed description of treatments and their abbreviations as used in the datasets, see text.](figures/funcab.png){#fig-design}

The experimental treatments were named by the functional group remaining, where *None* is gaps with all plants removed, *F* is only forbs, *G* only graminoids, *B* only bryophytes, *FG*, *FB*, and *GB* are the combinations of functional groups (forbs and graminoids, forbs and bryophytes, graminoids and bryophytes, and *All* are the control plots, with all functional groups present.

### Data collection

After eight years of functional group removal, data on microclimate, nutrient and carbon cycling, and the soil-food web including nematodes and microbes was collected. Most of the datasets were collected from all eight treatments, from three blocks at all twelve sites in 2022. Ecosystem carbon flux measurements were collected in 2017 and 2022 at nine sites (see below). Nematodes and available nutrients were only collected in five treatments (None, F, G, B, All), and available nutrients were collected in 2021.

*Aboveground biomass* was harvested in all plots in 2022, sorted by functional group (forbs, graminoids and bryophytes) and litter (i.e. dead non attached plant material), dried at 60°C for 48 h and weighed.

*Microclimate* We used Tomst loggers to continously measure ground temperatre and soil moisture between June and August 2022. 

*Nutrient cycling* Soil samples for C and N stocks...
Available nutrients were measured using Plant Root Simulator (PRSTM; Western Ag Innovations, Inc., Saskatoon, Canada). The probes were installed for 35 - 36 days between August and September 2021.

*Carbon cycling* In 2017 and 2022, ecosystem CO~2~ fluxes including Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) and Ecosystem Respiration (Reco) were measured in each plot at nine of the sites, excluding the three sites at the second wettest precipitation level (2100 mm annual precipitation; see @fig-design). NEE and Reco were measured using a closed loop chamber attached to an infrared gas analyzer (Li-840; LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). NEE was measured using the clear chamber, while for Reco fluxes were measured under dark conditions by covering the chamber with a dark tarp to block the sunlight.
Plant decomposition was measured by burrying site specific forb and graminoid litter between autumn 2021 and 2022. Two bags of 0.5-1g plant litter in nylon mesh bags were burried per plot and retreived after one year. The litter bags were dried at X°C, weighed and the mass loss caluclated. Fungal necromass decomposition was measured by growing mycelium of two ectomycorrhizal species, *Cenococcum geophilum* and *Suillus variegatus* (both native to the sites in our experiment), in the lab. The mycelium was homogenized and then processed in the same way as the plant litter.

*Nematode* Nematodes were extracted from 20 soil cores (1.7 cm diameter and up to 10 cm deep) per plot. The nematodes were extracted using a modified sugar flotation method based on Jenkins (1964). We counted all the fixed nematodes in every sample and identified 150 randomly chosen individuals to family level using an inverted microscope, and assigned putative feeding types according to Yeates 1993.

*Microbes* Peter!


For more details on the measurements and data cleaning see @vandvik2022role and Funder data paper. 

### Calculation of cosystem functions

We use `{r} n_distinct(big_data$response)` functions and properties as proxies for ecosystem functions @tbl-responses. The functions are grouped into five groups including microclimate, nutrient cycling, carbon cycling, nematodes, and microbes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-responses
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Groupd of functions.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
tar_load(big_data)

big_data |>
    mutate(
        group = factor(group, levels = c("microenvironment", "nutrient cycling", "carbon cycling", "nematodes", "microbes")),
        response = pretty_response_label(response)
    ) |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(response = paste(sort(unique(response)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(group) |>
    gt() |>
    tab_header(title = "Ecosystem functions by group") |>
    cols_label(group = "Group", response = "Ecosystem functions / responses")
```

For functions related to microclimate we calculated two variables related to temperature and drought. Daily temperature amplitude was calculated as the mean top 25% of the difference between maximum and minimum daily ground temperature. The drought index was calculated as the mean bottom 25% of the daily minimum soil moisture (driest days).

```{r}
#| label: eigenvalue
#| echo: false
tar_load(micronutrients_pca)

ev <- eigenvals(micronutrients_pca[[3]]) / sum(eigenvals(micronutrients_pca[[3]]))
```

We used five variable related to nutrient cycling: nitrogen and phosphorous stocks, available nitrogen (average of N0~3-~ and NH^4+^) and available phosphorous, and available micro nutrient. For the available micronutrients, we ran a principle component analysis (PCA) using the rda function in the vegan package (REF vegan, Oksanen) based on scaled and centered data. The first PC axis explained `{r} round(ev[1] * 100, 1)` % of the variation, and we used the first PC axis as a proxy for available micro nutrient.

Seven variables represented carbon cycling: decomposition of forb litter, and graminoid litter, ecosystem respiration gross primary productivity, melanised and non-melaniced fungal necromass decomposition. Decomposition was calculated as the weight loss of litter of necromass over one year. GPP was calculated by subtracting Reco from NEE.

We used seven variables on nematodes: the relative abundance of bacterivore, fungivore, plant, and predator feeder, bacteria:fungal feeder, maturity index, and plant parasite index. The nematode were classified into feeding groups based on (REF). In addition, we calculated the ratio of bacteria to fungi feeders. Finally, we calculated the maturity index and the plant parasite index [*add what they mean*].

We also used eight variables on microbes: the relative abundance of total bacteria and total fungi, ectomycorrhizal, root associated, saprotroph, yeast, and diamorphic fungi, and the bacteria:fungi ratio.


### Standardization and calculations

Functions were if possible converted, so that higher values mean higher ecosystem functioning or variables go from slow to fast processes/strategies. The plant parasite index, and maturity index as well as GPP were inverted. The bacteria to fungi ratio, also indicates a slow to fast strategy. For functions that contain negative values (i.e. NEE, available nutrients), we added the absolute minimum value plus one. For functions with a strongly skewed distribution, we log transformed the data, except for ratios, where we used the logit transformation. We then standardized the values of each funciton to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, to remove differences in measurement scale between the variables.

To calculate average multifunctionality, we used the absolute values of each function and then calculated the mean of absolute standardized values across all individual functions as $MF_a = \frac{1}{F} \sum_{i=1}^{F} abs(f_i)$, where $F$ is the number of functions and $f_i$ is a measure of function $i$.

#### Testing the effect of functional group remaining, biomass and climate on ecosystem functions

The models were run for nine sites and five treatments.

We ran three different linear mixed-effects models to test the effect of functional group remaining, climate and biomass on ecosystem functions. We excluded the interaction of temperature and precipitation to simplify the model.

Model 1: To test the effect of functional group removed and climate
function ~ functional group remaining x (T + P) + (1/siteID)

Model 2: to test if the biomass of the functional groups matters we add remaining bioamss to model 1
function ~ functional group remaining + (T x P) + biomass + (1/siteID)

Model 3: to test if the amount of biomass from differet functional groups matter, we ran a model with functional group biomass and climate
function ~ biomassF + biomassG + biomassB + (T x P) + (1/siteID)

We ran these full models and a main effects model only to see if the interactions were important. The main effects model included the interaction of temperature and precipitation.

To the best model for each function we did the following:

To find the best model for each function, we compared the AIC values of the six models. The most parsimonous model was the one with the lowest AIC value.

We calculated the conditional and marginal R^2^ for each model. To test if the variance explained changes when adding biomass (model 1 vs. model 2) or functional group biomass (model 2 vs. model 3) to the model, we ran a paired Wilcoxon test between the conditional or marginal R^2^ from model 1 and 2 as well as model 2 and 3. We also ran a linear regression, testing if the relationship between the R^2^ of the two models differ from the 1:1 line.

To test if the estimates (slopes) of the different model term change when adding biomass (model 1 vs. model 2) or functional group biomass (model 2 vs. model 3) to the model, we ran a paired Wilcoxon test between the estimates from these models. We also ran a linear regression, testing if the relationship between the estimates of the two models differ from the 1:1 line.

We ran the same tests comparing the R^2^ and estimates between the full and main effects models.
